opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and it's one we think about a lot. I'd frame it as a question of what level of abstraction gives you the most useful learning signal per unit of compute and data.

Predicting the full future sensor stream, essentially building a world model that generates future camera frames or lidar sweeps, is very appealing in principle. It's self-supervised, so you can train it on huge amounts of driving logs without labels, and in theory it captures everything: the agents, the road, the weather, the lighting. But a lot of the capacity of such a model goes into things that don't matter much for driving. Getting the exact texture of a building or the reflection on a wet road right is expensive, and it doesn't really help you decide whether to yield to that pedestrian.

Predicting other road users' motion is much more targeted. You're working in a structured representation of agents, their trajectories, their interactions, the map. That's where much of the hard reasoning in driving lives: what will this cyclist do, will that car cut in, how will others react to my actions. It's compact, it's directly tied to the planning problem, and you can evaluate it in ways that are meaningful for safety.

So in practice I don't see these as competing. Sensor-level prediction is a powerful way to learn rich representations and to build realistic simulators, especially for capturing the long tail of things your structured abstraction might miss. Behavior prediction is where you want precision and interpretability, because that's what feeds decision making. The interesting direction is combining them: using large-scale generative pretraining to learn good features and world knowledge, then grounding and fine-tuning on the structured, agent-centric tasks that actually determine whether you drive safely. And critically, you want those predictions to be reactive and conditioned on your own plan, because driving is a multi-agent game, not a passive forecasting problem.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a great question, and I'd say it's one of the central tensions in how we think about representation learning for driving right now.

Let me start with motion prediction, because that's where a lot of the field, including us at Waymo, has invested heavily. Predicting the future behavior of other agents is extremely valuable because it's directly tied to the decision the vehicle actually has to make. The planner cares about where the pedestrian is going to be in three seconds, whether that car is going to cut in, whether the cyclist is going to yield. So when you supervise on agent trajectories, you're supervising on something that is almost perfectly aligned with the downstream task. It's compact, it's interpretable, and you can evaluate it in a meaningful way. If your motion forecasts are good, you can usually explain why the car behaved well or badly.

The downside is that it's a lossy abstraction. You've decided in advance what matters, which is boxes with trajectories, and anything that doesn't fit that ontology gets thrown away. Debris on the road, a door opening on a parked car, a traffic cone that's been knocked into the lane, subtle cues about driver intent that show up in how a vehicle is drifting within its lane before it changes lanes. Those things are all in the sensor data, and a system trained only to predict agent motion may never learn to represent them.

Predicting the full future sensor stream, whether that's camera, lidar, or some latent representation of it, is appealing precisely because it doesn't require you to make those choices. It's a form of self-supervision that scales with data. You don't need labelers to decide what the ontology is. The model has to understand geometry, dynamics, occlusion, and how agents interact, because otherwise it can't predict what the world is going to look like. In principle that's a much richer learning signal, and you can get it from essentially every mile you drive.

But there are real problems with it. The first is that most of the bits in a future sensor frame are irrelevant to driving. Predicting exactly how the leaves on a tree move or how the texture on a building looks from a slightly different angle consumes model capacity and doesn't help you avoid a collision. So you have an allocation issue. The loss is dominated by things you don't care about, and the things you do care about, like the precise position of a small pedestrian at fifty meters, are a tiny fraction of the signal. The second problem is multimodality. The future is uncertain, and pixel-level or point-level reconstruction losses tend to average over that uncertainty unless you're careful, which gives you blurry, unrealistic predictions. And the third is evaluation. If your sensor prediction gets better, does your driving get better? That link is much harder to establish than it is for trajectory prediction.

So the way I'd frame it is that these aren't really competing. The question is what you use each one for. I think of sensor or latent future prediction as a pretraining and representation objective. It's how you get a model that has broad, general understanding of the scene, including the long tail of things you never thought to label. Then agent-centric motion prediction, along with planning objectives, is how you shape that representation toward the decisions that actually matter and how you verify it's working. Increasingly the interesting work is in the middle, predicting the future in a learned latent space rather than raw pixels, so that the model can decide what's worth representing, while still grounding that latent space with explicit supervision on agents, lanes, and the ego plan.

If I had to say where I'd put my marginal effort today, I'd say the agent prediction and planning side still gives you more reliable improvements in safety-critical behavior per unit of work. But the ceiling of that approach is determined by the ontology you chose, and I think the way you break through that ceiling is with the more general, self-supervised future prediction. So I'd weigh them not as either-or but as a question of which stage of the pipeline each belongs in.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re complementary, but they emphasize different things. Predicting other road users’ motion gives you a fairly direct connection to the driving task: Where might this pedestrian go? Is this vehicle going to yield? And how should your own behavior change in response? You want a distribution of possible futures, because often there isn’t a single outcome you can confidently predict.

Predicting the future sensor stream is a broader learning objective. It can help you learn representations from large amounts of unlabeled driving data, including aspects of the scene that an explicit motion representation might leave out. But it also asks the model to spend capacity on details that may have little relevance to a driving decision. A visually plausible future doesn’t necessarily mean you’ve captured the subtle interaction that matters for safety.

So I would judge both by how much they improve planning and closed-loop driving. Can the model anticipate a consequential event, represent uncertainty, and choose an appropriate action? I’d also want predictions to account for what our vehicle might do, because other road users react to us. The value is ultimately in helping the vehicle make better decisions, rather than just producing a more accurate-looking forecast.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re complementary, but they serve somewhat different purposes. Predicting the motion of other road users gives you a representation that’s very directly connected to driving: Where might this pedestrian go? Is this vehicle going to yield? What should I do in response? You can focus your modeling capacity on the uncertainty that matters for those decisions.

Predicting the future sensor stream is a much broader learning problem. The attraction is that you can learn from large amounts of data without having to explicitly label everything. To predict what you’ll observe next, the model has to learn something about geometry, motion, and how the world evolves. But it also has to predict a lot of detail that may have little relevance to driving. A visually plausible future isn’t necessarily a future that captures the important safety considerations.

So I wouldn’t judge these approaches just by how good their predictions look. I’d ask how much they improve the driving system. Does the representation help you anticipate an unusual interaction? Does it capture multiple possible outcomes? And, particularly, does it help you reason about how those outcomes change depending on your own actions? That’s where prediction becomes useful for planning. You can use a broad predictive objective to learn representations, while still having more targeted objectives that connect that learning to the driving task.
